beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new, it's a title

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: Sharing an agent isn't the point. Context, skill, output or interface is what travels.

beats.trigger: Walk in with one example where people had access to a tool or process but real use did not follow.
beats.got: nothing new. I have a dozen of those, the confluence rollout for one.

beats.trigger: **Name** the likely adoption failure before it happens, including the social failure that's hardest to see
beats.got: nothing new, it's a list of verbs and I'd rather get to the build.

beats.trigger: And what makes you hesitate about actually handing this to them?
beats.got: I haven't asked myself that. I just build things and hand them over.

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: Jobs-to-be-done framing. I know it from product work, and it's a bit textbook.

beats.trigger: If the agent ranges too wide, interrupt with *"tell me what you've found so far, narrow to the files that bear on this teammate, then continue."*
beats.got: The agent over-reads or under-reads, and I steer it with one line. Useful, small.

beats.trigger: If the reason is merely *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: I pick the shape by the outcome, not by what infra we have. That's my usual mistake.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a handoff to the next exercise.

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a setup beat.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Look for the one obstacle that holds the others in place, not the first technical limit.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: My sales-team setup would have a great technical plan and an empty people plan. I can see that.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact
beats.got: nothing new, it's another handoff.

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are guesses until someone tests them.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: Flip the question from how I get them to adopt it to what must be true for them to drop what they use now. That's new to me.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: Write three failure stories, then turn the strongest into one named conversation and one test. A premortem, and it's concrete.

beats.trigger: Test the switch, not the solution.
beats.got: A recap line. It's good, but I'd have gotten there anyway.

beats.trigger: The rest of this is about the person on the other end of your plan.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a framing sentence.

beats.trigger: A good interview finds a third outcome past speed and quality: a dependency removed, an anxiety gone, a scope widened.
beats.got: Mostly a repeat of the exercise, plus the third-outcome idea, which is a decent nuance.

beats.trigger: Hand someone the agent file and they run it, get a generic answer, and quietly stop.
beats.got: The agent file is a page of instructions. The value sits in the memory and corrections around it, so a copied file gives generic output.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks copy easily. Who answers for it doesn't. I never asked who maintains my builds.

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: We report seats activated as adoption. That's access, not absorption.

beats.trigger: *we know more than we can tell.*
beats.got: Polanyi quote. A bit philosophical, and I got the point without it.

beats.trigger: The interface is the first piece whose shape depends on somebody whose calendar you do not control.
beats.got: The interface is the first piece I can't control alone.

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: A multi-agent org redesign still died because leadership hadn't done the analysis themselves and priorities moved. That's an org-wide failure mode I haven't hit.

beats.trigger: Somebody they trust has to have used it first and said so.
beats.got: The switch conditions are small and specific: land where they look, be right the first time, have a trusted person vouch.

beats.trigger: Whether they pick it up is their decision, made for their own reasons, on a Tuesday you will not be in the room for.
beats.got: I can hand over the pieces but not the decision to use them.

beats.trigger: A missing name is a finding: it marks the part of this that is not built yet
beats.got: If I can't name who owns it, it isn't built yet, however finished the tech is.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews, rewrites the sharing artifact in place, and reports what changed.
beats.got: Standard review-and-rewrite step. I'd probably skip it.

beats.trigger: Save the conversation. It's the bridge to when work resumes.
beats.got: nothing new, housekeeping.

beats.trigger: Access is easy; absorption is scarce.
beats.got: A summary of what I just read.

beats.trigger: Test one assumption. Ask for one name. Talk to one person.
beats.got: Module 8 expects real contact with one person. That's a bit slow for me, but fair.

beats.trigger: What comes back from that contact is Module 8's raw material.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a pointer to Module 8.

take_homes: Ask what has to be true for someone to drop what they use now before building them anything. I never ask that.
A shared agent without a named owner is only three of four parts. I need a name for who maintains it.
Access and absorption are different numbers, and we only track access.

monday.move: Before building the sales setup, ask the head of sales one question: how do you do forecasting and pipeline reviews today? Fill in the people-plan names for my confluence-for-everyone idea. If I can't name an owner, I don't build it.
monday.who: One person on the sales team, probably the sales lead, and whoever would own it after me
monday.when: Monday or Tuesday, a 20-minute chat, before I touch the weekend build
monday.stop_condition: Nobody on sales can say what job it would do for them, or no owner can be named.
monday.blocker: Nobody outside engineering asked for it. I'll be tempted to build first anyway because it's fun.

misconception.why: The module never made me slow down on checking output. It was all about adoption and people, so 'checking is for beginners' wasn't challenged. The 'accountability doesn't copy' beat made me doubt the 'agent is good so output is good' side a little, but not enough to say shaken.

one_line: Good for anyone about to roll an agent out to non-engineers, and the Finnish value-stream story is the best part. It's slow on the exercise steps if you already run agents, and it doesn't touch verification at all.
